title: Stage-1 minimal discriminator: recency decay versus valid-time gating on non-latest-authoritative clauses
research_question: On clause-versioned amended legal text, does the published recency-decay hybrid already match a valid-time (as-of) gate on version contamination and point-in-time recovery, or does decay fail specifically on queries whose authoritative version is not the latest?
hypothesis: On amended legal clauses whose authoritative (in-force) version is old while a recent near-duplicate version exists, the published recency-decay hybrid selects the wrong version substantially more often than a valid-time (as-of) gate; on queries whose authoritative version is the latest, the two perform equivalently. If decay matches the gate on the discriminating subset, recency is a sufficient proxy for validity in this domain.
proposed_method: Curate clause version chains from a public consolidated legal corpus with per-version validity dates. For each chain, construct time-stamped queries whose target date lies inside an older version's validity window and whose clause has a recent near-duplicate version, so decay and validity make opposite predictions; also include latest-gold and no-version-in-force queries. Run five retrieval conditions (BM25, dense, hybrid RRF, hybrid+decay at swept rates, and a recency-only ranker) each with and without a post-hoc valid-time gate, scoring retrieval against version-identity gold labels. Reuse the retrieval and metric plumbing patterns of the public RMA regulatory QA harness (same sparse/dense/RRF structure, structure-aware chunking, ROUGE-free retrieval metrics), then extend with version chains and target dates, which that harness lacks. Stage 1 is retrieval-only and CPU-bound; Stage 2 adds the fixed reader and the answer-differential screen.
baselines: Published three-signal hybrid (lexical + dense + exponential decay) with a tuned decay rate - the strong, directly comparable baseline
BM25 sparse retrieval only and dense bge-small retrieval only - budget-matched controls
Hybrid RRF without any temporal term
Random temporal assignment control (random validity intervals)
datasets: Stage 1 (retrieval-only, CPU): a small hand-curated set of clause version chains from a public consolidated legal/regulatory corpus with machine-readable entry-into-force and applicability dates, targeting roughly 100-200 time-stamped queries of which at least 50 are non-latest-gold
Corpus criterion: clauses with at least two versions and a documented validity interval per version
Stage 2 (optional): add the reader LLM and the answer-differential screen on the same chains
Not used at this stage: ESG and financial-filing corpora (domain mismatch), the static RMA regulatory corpus (no versioning or target dates)
workloads: Discriminating-case queries: target date inside an old validity window, with a recent near-duplicate version of the same clause in the candidate pool
Latest-gold queries: authoritative version is the most recent (expected equivalence control)
No-version-in-force queries where abstention is correct
Boundary queries: target date equal to an entry-into-force or applicability date
Deep-chain clauses with three or more versions to test whether contamination grows with chain depth
hardware: Stage 1 is CPU-only: BM25 plus BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 embeddings on a few hundred clause versions, comfortably runnable on a laptop. Stage 2 optionally uses one GPU or a hosted reader LLM with cached responses.
metrics: Primary: version contamination - fraction of retrieved passages not in force at the target date
Primary: clause-level point-in-time recovery - fraction of queries whose top-ranked passage is the in-force version
Primary: version confusion - selected version differs from gold version
Diagnostic: discriminating-case counts and the gap between decay and gate on that subset
Diagnostic: nDCG@k / Recall@k against version-identity gold labels
Diagnostic: contamination under decay as a function of the age gap between the in-force version and the latest version
Stage 2 only: answer accuracy on the answer-differential subset and the screen pass rate
ablations: Decay rate sweep, reporting the best case for decay (including per-query-type tuning) so the comparison is not an artifact of a fixed rate
Hard valid-time gate vs graded gate with a tie-break
Validity-interval boundary handling: inclusive vs half-open, same-day amendment and applicability dates
Retrieval depth k and chunk granularity (whole clause vs sub-clause fragments)
Discriminating-case subset only (old in-force version plus recent near-duplicate)
controls: Same chunking, k, embedding model and candidate pool across all arms
Version-identity gold labels rather than answer strings
Every arm scored on the identical query set and target dates
Per-stratum reporting (discriminating case vs latest-gold) instead of a pooled average
Seeds fixed; rankings released per query so metrics can be recomputed
confounders_addressed: Decay and gate may agree because the authoritative version is usually the latest - addressed by the discriminating-case subset (old in-force window with a recent near-duplicate)
Answers may be identical across versions, hiding retrieval errors - Stage 1 scores retrieval at version-identity level with no reader
Decay rate choice could favour either arm - swept and reported at its best, including per-query-type tuning
Shallow amendment chains would leave little to test - minimum-version-count curation criterion
Date granularity and boundary conventions could drive the result - tested explicitly
Long-lived in-force clauses demoted purely by age - measured directly on old-window queries
expected_outcomes: On the discriminating subset, the decay hybrid shows materially higher version contamination and lower point-in-time recovery than the valid-time gate, because decay is monotone in age and demotes long-lived in-force clauses; on the latest-gold subset the two are equivalent, which is reported as the expected boundary condition. Semantic-only retrieval is intermediate. If decay tuned per query type closes the gap, that is reported as evidence that decay can approximate validity when its rate is effectively condition-dependent.
failure_conditions: The decay hybrid matches the gate on the discriminating subset within confidence intervals - recency is a sufficient proxy and the direction is falsified
Semantic-only retrieval already achieves near-zero version contamination - the problem premise fails and there is nothing for a temporal term to fix

No accessible corpus yields enough clauses with documented per-version validity intervals - the benchmark is infeasible and the direction should be dropped rather than approximated with document-level dates
The gate's advantage vanishes once the decay rate is tuned per query type - the validity-versus-recency distinction reduces to rate calibration
Contamination differences exist but the answer-differential screen is empty (no query's answer depends on version) - the finding is metric-only
reproducibility_notes: No execution spec is attached. The only open implementation found (RMA regulatory QA benchmark repository) is a Jupyter notebook that requires downloading third-party RMA PDFs and setting an OpenRouter API key, computes metrics live in-notebook rather than emitting a JSON results file, and - decisively - has a static corpus with no versioning or target dates, so it cannot be run to test this hypothesis; it is reusable for chunking, index-building and evaluation patterns only. When built: pin and publish the corpus snapshot and amendment metadata source, release the version chains, validity intervals and query-stratum assignments, fix all seeds, hold embeddings/k/chunking fixed across arms, sweep and report the decay rate at its best, publish per-query rankings, and report paired bootstrap confidence intervals plus both natural-prevalence-weighted and oversampled estimates.
